mstts:express-as.prosody: Have you ever caught yourself defending a decision, even when deep down, you sensed it might not have been the right one? We all do it—sometimes without even realizing. Self-justification, that quiet voice inside that helps us explain away our choices, is always at work beneath the surface. Together, we’re about to uncover how these everyday habits shape the way we remember, believe, and even talk about our lives. In Mistakes Were Made, but Not by Me: Why We Justify Foolish Beliefs, Bad Decisions, and Hurtful Acts, Carol Tavris shines a light on the hidden forces of cognitive dissonance and self-deception—those little tricks our minds play to keep our self-image intact. Why do we double down on our choices, even when the facts don’t line up? What makes it so hard to admit when we’re wrong, or to let go of beliefs that just don’t hold up? As we explore Tavris’s insights, we’ll see how memory, emotion, and identity all connect, and why it feels so risky to own up to our mistakes. But there’s hope—because understanding these patterns isn’t about blaming ourselves or others. It’s about discovering new ways to grow, to heal, and to build better connections, both with ourselves and with the people around us. So, let’s set out on this journey together, and get curious about what really shapes the stories we tell—about the world, and about ourselves.
